newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian media gloss over Yeltsin doctor's remarks.
newsitem.headline: Russian media gloss over Yeltsin doctor's remarks.

text.p: A top surgeon's suggestion that President Boris Yeltsin has probably had a third, unnannounced heart attack made headlines abroad but was largely ignored by Russia's media at the weekend.

Renat Akchurin, who is helping prepare Yeltsin for surgery, said in interviews with Western media that the president probably had the heart attack just before he was re-elected in July and may not be well enough to withstand heart surgery now.
Russian television and radio channels made little mention of the news, burying it low in bulletins when they referred to it at all. The Kremlin maintained a strict silence.

More than five years after the collapse of communist rule and strict media controls, Russian editors remain cautious of any news that relates to the president's health and could have a bearing on the country's fragile democracy.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, who says he is best placed to be Russia's next leader, portrays the liberal media as being part of a conspiracy of silence over Yeltsin's health which peaked during the presidential race but has continued.

"People were deceived by NTV and ORT (television channels), and by newspapers that wrote about firm handshakes," Zyuganov, who lost a presidential election to Yeltsin less than three months ago, told a news conference on Friday.

Media speculation about Yeltsin's health has increased since he secured re-election on July 3. Some reports, including an investigation by the weekly Itogi news magazine, reveal that reporters have made major efforts to find out the truth.
But the weekend media coverage pointed to Russian editors' continued nervousness on the issue and mistrust of Western speculation over Yeltsin's condition.

ORT (Russian Public Television), which is partly owned by the government and is Russia's biggest network, reported Akchurin's comment made to U.S. channel ABC that Yeltsin, 65, had probably had his third heart attack in 12 months.

It said it had triggered "a new wave of journalists' fuss around President Yeltsin's health" and pointed out that the doctor was speaking in English. It suggested this could have resulted in some inexactness of terminology.

NTV, a commercial channel, reported Akchurin's separate remarks to Reuters that Yeltsin may not be able to withstand the planned bypass surgery and called them "sensational". It did not mention the report of a third heart attack.
The main news agencies, Itar-Tass and Interfax, did not mention Akchurin's remarks at all.

"Of course the health of the head of state is not just a medical question, but also a political one," the liberal newspaper Izvestia wrote earlier this month after Yeltsin announced he would have heart surgery.
"But at the same time it is difficult to avoid the idea that a natural preoccupation with this question has turned into gross interference in the president's internal affairs," it said.
Uncertainty and caution over coverage is not surprising in a country where the media long needed official permission before going into print during communist rule.
Some liberal journalists acknowledge that fears of the communists returning to power clouded their election coverage. There is little doubt they are still plagued by such concerns.
"The mass media by their very nature have become Yeltsin's natural allies," ORT spokesman Alexei Pushkov commented during the election campaign.
"With Yeltsin they know where they stand and, for all his faults, he has not infringed on media freedoms."
